title: Birthday Problem & Hash Collisions
prompt: How many people need to be in a room for >50% chance two share a birthday? Derive the approximation. Follow-up: how does this relate to hash collision risk when bucketing order IDs?

title: Pricing a Dice Game
prompt: A game pays $1 for each roll until the first 6, then stops. What fair upfront price would you pay to play? A trader offers $3.50 — do you take it? What if variance matters and you have a bankroll limit?

title: Call Option Bounds & Intuition
prompt: Stock S=$100, strike K=$100, 1 month to expiry, no dividends. Without Black-Scholes: what are lower/upper bounds on a European call price? How do delta and gamma behave as S moves? What assumptions break in real markets?

title: Market Making Spread
prompt: You market-make a stock with volatile order flow. How do you set bid-ask spread? What inputs drive widening? Explain adverse selection and inventory risk in plain language with a numeric example.
hints: Spread vs volatility and flow toxicity.

title: Random Walk Hitting Time
prompt: Simple symmetric random walk on integers starting at 0. What is the probability of hitting +5 before -3? Explain via first-step analysis or gambler's ruin. Why does this matter for PnL drawdown modeling?

title: Regression Overfit in Factor Research
prompt: You fit 50 factors on 10 years of daily data and pick the top 3 by in-sample Sharpe. Why is this dangerous? Design a validation protocol that a skeptical PM would accept.

title: Onsite: Invent a Winning Theory
prompt: Two players alternately name a distinct integer from 1..9. First to own three numbers that sum to 15 wins (like a race to a magic-square line). You go first. Is there a winning strategy? Decompose on the fly: map to a known game if helpful, argue with cases, and state your conclusion. Follow-up: if the target sum were 14 instead, how does your theory change?

title: Data Exercise: Concise Trading Report
prompt:
You are given (pretend) 30 days of options-market quotes: columns timestamp, underlying, strike, expiry, bid, ask, mid, volume, and a flag for quote source. Prompt: 'Is there a tradable edge after costs, and what breaks it?'
Write a report outline (not 200 graphs): (A) 3 hypotheses you'd test first, (B) at most 5 figures/tables you'd actually include and why each earns its slot, (C) how you'd answer a senior who asks 'why doesn't your analysis see adverse selection / stale quotes / regime change?', (D) a one-paragraph results-first summary you could present to a math PhD on a fly-out.
hints: Name failure modes before they do.

title: Tech Screen: Basic Programming Still Matters
prompt: Implement (or clearly pseudo-code) a function that, given a list of trade prices and a window w, returns the rolling mean — correctly handling the first w-1 points (define your convention). Discuss time/space complexity and one edge case (empty list, w larger than n, NaNs). This is the 'basic programming' bar that still appears in prop-shop tech rounds even when AI coding tools are common.
